annotations.keyFindings: On 24 randomised wards, tiering raised acceptance of high-severity interruptive alerts from 11 to 29 percent and cut interruptive alerts from 8.2 to 1.9 per 100 orders, without more harmful moderate-interaction combinations on pharmacist review.
annotations.limitations: Two hospitals; rotation contamination; no direct adverse drug event outcome.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 9 hospitals, override rates were 90 to 96 percent, similar for high- and low-severity alerts, and rose with alerts per shift.
Across 27 studies, tiering and suppression reduced alert volume; only 4 measured patient outcomes and none showed a clear change in adverse drug events.
annotations.limitations: Mostly before-and-after designs with concurrent changes.

annotations.keyFindings: Two pharmacists judged 87 percent of 1,000 overridden alerts appropriate (kappa 0.71); override rate alone misclassifies appropriate overrides.
annotations.limitations: One organisation's definition; four minutes per alert.

annotations.keyFindings: Randomising prescribers under ward-set displays exposed 40 percent of orders to the other arm; ward randomisation cut this below 10 percent at a design effect of about 2.1.
Surveillance of 2,400 dispensed moderate-interaction combinations after tiering judged 14 harmful (0.6 percent), similar to the previous year; potassium-raising combinations dominated.
annotations.limitations: One hospital; before-and-after comparison of harm.

annotations.keyFindings: Seventy-two percent of 410 responding prescribers overrode alerts without reading them at least weekly; they supported tiering if high-severity alerts stayed interruptive.

claims.text: In a cluster randomised trial on 24 wards, 29 percent of high-severity interruptive alerts were accepted with a tiered display against 11 percent with the standard display.
claims.passage: With tiering, 29 percent of high-severity interruptive alerts were accepted, compared with 11 percent under the standard display.
claims.interpretation: Gives the planning values for the primary comparison; contamination may have diluted it.

claims.text: When displays were set by ward but prescribers were randomised, 40 percent of orders were exposed to the other arm; ward randomisation cut this to under 10 percent at a design effect of about 2.1.
claims.passage: Randomising wards reduced exposure to the other arm to under 10 percent but needed a design effect of about 2.1 for the same number of orders.
claims.interpretation: Randomise wards, stratified by hospital and specialty.

claims.text: Pharmacist surveillance of 2,400 dispensed moderate-interaction combinations after tiering judged 14 harmful (0.6 percent), a rate similar to the year before.
claims.passage: They judged 14 as having caused or contributed to harm (0.6 percent), a rate similar to the year before tiering.
claims.interpretation: Targeted surveillance of suppressed combinations is a workable balancing measure.

claims.text: Two pharmacists judged 87 percent of 1,000 overridden alerts appropriate, with good agreement (kappa 0.71).
claims.passage: They judged 87 percent of overrides appropriate, with good agreement (kappa 0.71).
claims.interpretation: Use appropriate response (accepted or appropriately overridden) as the primary outcome rather than raw override rates.

claims.text: Only 4 of 27 studies of alert fatigue interventions measured patient outcomes, and none found a clear change in adverse drug events.
claims.passage: Only 4 studies measured patient outcomes, and none found a clear change in adverse drug events.
claims.interpretation: Do not promise an adverse drug event effect; measure harm as a balancing outcome.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One cluster randomised trial found tiering raised acceptance of high-severity alerts from 11 to 29 percent and cut interruptions fourfold, with no rise in harmful moderate combinations. Override rates are uniformly high and uninformative on their own; pharmacist-judged appropriateness is a reliable alternative outcome. Ward randomisation avoids most contamination when displays are ward settings. Surveillance after tiering found harm from suppressed moderate interactions at about the previous rate. No study shows an effect on adverse drug events.
gradeRationale: One moderate-quality cluster trial with contamination, a simulation study and observational work; consistent direction for prescriber response, low certainty for patient outcomes.
summary: Seven records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low.
